name: Mortgage payoff
seoTitle: Mortgage payoff Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Mortgage payoff: work out mortgage term from the interest rate and on the day of. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Mortgage payoff calculator the interest rate, on the day of and the extra payment and it returns mortgage term. It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Mortgage payoff calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mortgage payoff calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mortgage term in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the interest capitalization method and the payment frequency (Extra payment specification)); then you give on the day of (Current mortgage specification), on the day of (Extra payment specification) and the amortization schedule from; then you type in the interest rate, the extra payment, the one-time extra payment and the pmi.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mortgage payoff calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

N=the natural log of (payment gen ÷ (payment gen − eq p × mortgage amount)) ÷ the natural log of (eq p + 1)
Eq p=((interest capitalization method + interest rate) ÷ interest capitalization method, interest capitalization method ÷ payment frequency) − 1
N=payment frequency × mortgage term
Q2=payment gen × payment frequency ÷ payment accelerated
Payment=(payment accelerated × Ct2 + payment gen × Ct1 + extra payment)
Mortgage term=(1 ÷ 12) × n monthly

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mortgage payoff calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the interest rate, on the day of and the extra payment — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mortgage payoff calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mortgage term, derived from the interest rate, on the day of and the extra payment. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mortgage payoff calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the interest rate, on the day of and the extra payment, which is 26 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mortgage amount in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mortgage amount opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Down payment percentage = 0.1667. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mortgage payoff calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
